new_statements.quote: Pitch is phonemic in both dialects: high tone is marked by the acute accent; low tone is unmarked. [p. 113] ... a lengthening of the preceding vowel is also part of the shift and, in Atsina, a falling pitch on the lengthened vowel. [p. 114] ... Short vowels with low pitch in non-final syllables are subject to syncope in Atsina when located between a non-clustered consonant and an intervocalic /ʔ/ or /h/. [p. 117; the scanned layer garbles the first phoneme as 'PI']
new_statements.citation: Taylor, Allan R. 1967. Some observations on a comparative Arapaho-Atsina lexicon. Contributions to Anthropology: Linguistics I (Algonquian), National Museum of Canada Bulletin 214, pp. 113-127 (open reissue: Algonquian Papers - Archive 1, https://ojs.library.carleton.ca/index.php/ALGQP/article/view/432)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Atsina (Gros Ventre) has phonemic pitch, high vs. low, marked lexically with an acute accent on high-pitch vowels; long vowels can carry a falling pitch; low-pitch short vowels are the ones that syncopate. Taylor gives no rule for where the high pitch falls in the word and does not use the notion of stress at all; §2.0 explicitly excludes the prosodic differences between Arapaho and Atsina from the paper.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the paper says (§2.0) that prosodic features differ between Arapaho and Atsina but are not collated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical pitch on citation forms from Taylor's own 1960s field recordings (Fort Belknap). The alternative catalog reading is 'tone-language-no-stress-statement' (Taylor's own wording is 'high tone'/'low tone'); 'pitch-accent' is chosen because the Arapahoan literature (Cowell & Moss 2008 for Arapaho) treats the system as pitch accent and Taylor's two-level, lexically marked description is the same object.
new_statements.identity_note: Taylor's 'Atsina' = Gros Ventre of Fort Belknap, Montana (gros1243), from his own 1960s field tapes; he treats Arapaho and Atsina as two dialects of one Arapahoan language. The modern name Aaniiih / White Clay (Cowell & Brockie) is the same variety. Brockie & Cowell 2017 note men's vs women's pronunciation differences (č vs c), not relevant to pitch.

sources.note: §2.1 p. 113: phoneme inventories of Arapaho and Atsina, then 'Pitch is phonemic in both dialects: high tone is marked by the acute accent; low tone is unmarked.' (verified against the page image); p. 114: in Atsina a falling pitch appears on a vowel lengthened by the *-iθ- shift; p. 117 §4.3: short vowels with low pitch in non-final syllables syncopate in Atsina. No positional rule; stress is not mentioned; §2.0 says prosodic differences between the dialects are not collated.

sources.citation: Brockie, Terry & Andrew Cowell. 2017. Introduction: Aaniiih language. In Brockie & Cowell (comps.), Aaniiih/Gros Ventre Stories (First Nations Language Readers), pp. xv-xxii. Regina: University of Regina Press. DOI 10.1515/9780889774810-003 (open access per Unpaywall; De Gruyter site blocks bots, copy taken from Wayback 2025-05-03)
sources.note: Gives only the consonant and vowel inventory (b, c, č, h, k, n, s, t, θ, w, y, ʔ; a, e, i, ɔ, o, u) and rough pronunciations; nothing on pitch, accent or stress; 'Details about pronunciation can be found in Allan Taylor's 1994 Gros Ventre Dictionary' (p. xv); footnote names the CSILW 'Gros Ventre/White Clay Student Reference Grammar, Part One'.

sources.note: K-4 curriculum; no linguistic description; only the remark that Gros Ventre 'has a lot of sounds, accents, and inflections that can not be written down except by a linguist'.

sources.citation: Kroeber, A. L. 1916. Arapaho dialects. University of California Publications in American Archaeology and Ethnology 12(3): 71-138. archive.org item arapahodialects00kroerich
sources.note: Part II 'Phonetic Elements' pp. 83-84 (covers Gros Ventre too) and Part III 'Notes on Gros Ventre: Phonetics' p. 131: no statement on accent placement; only 'Final vowels, unless long or accented, are surd or whispered' (p. 83) and that final-vowel devoicing is more complete in Gros Ventre (p. 84).
